questions.title: How do type narrowing and discriminated unions work in TypeScript?
questions.quick: Narrowing is how the compiler refines a union to a more specific type inside a branch, using typeof, instanceof, in, equality, truthiness or custom type guards. A discriminated union gives each variant a literal tag field such as kind or type, so a switch on that tag narrows the whole object. I add a never-based exhaustiveness check so adding a new variant produces a compile error wherever it is not handled, which makes state machines and API results safe.
questions.revision: Narrowing refines unions via typeof, in, instanceof and guards; discriminated unions use a literal tag, and a never check enforces exhaustive handling.
followUps: How do you write a custom type guard safely?
What does the never type represent?
How do discriminated unions model API responses?

diagrams.title: Narrowing a discriminated union
diagrams.alt: A union value is checked on its status tag; each branch gives the compiler a specific variant, and a default branch assigns the leftover to never to enforce exhaustiveness.

questions.title: How do generics work: constraints, defaults and inference?
questions.quick: Generics let a function or type work over many types while keeping the relationship between inputs and outputs. A constraint with extends limits what is allowed so I can use known properties, a default type parameter supplies a fallback, and inference usually works out the type argument from the call so callers rarely write it. I keep generics minimal, name parameters meaningfully, and avoid generics that appear only once, because they add noise without safety.
questions.revision: Generics relate input and output types; extends constrains, defaults supply fallbacks, inference fills arguments; use them only when they express a real relationship.
followUps: What does keyof do and how is it used with generics?
When must you pass explicit type arguments?
Why is a generic that appears once a smell?

diagrams.title: Generic inference at a call site
diagrams.alt: The compiler reads the argument types at a call, infers the type parameter, checks it against any constraint, and substitutes it into the return type.

questions.title: What are the main utility types, and how do mapped and conditional types work?
questions.quick: Utility types transform existing types: Partial makes properties optional, Required the reverse, Pick selects keys, Omit removes them, Record builds a map type, ReturnType and Parameters extract function types, and Awaited unwraps promises. They are built from mapped types, which iterate over keys, and conditional types, which choose a type with extends and can use infer. I use them to derive types from a single source of truth instead of duplicating definitions.
questions.revision: Partial, Required, Pick, Omit, Record, ReturnType, Awaited derive types; they are built from mapped types over keys and conditional types with infer.
questions.detailed:
Utility types let you **derive** types rather than copy them, so one definition changes everything that depends on it.

## Common utilities

| Utility | Result |
|---|---|
| Partial<T> | All properties optional (PATCH payloads) |
| Required<T> | All properties required |
| Readonly<T> | All properties readonly |
| Pick<T, K> | Only keys K |
| Omit<T, K> | Everything except K (for example, without id) |
| Record<K, V> | Object with keys K and values V |
| ReturnType<F> | Return type of function F |
| Parameters<F> | Tuple of F's parameter types |
| Awaited<T> | Resolved type of a promise |
| NonNullable<T> | Removes null and undefined |

```ts
interface User { id: string; email: string; role: 'admin' | 'user' }

type CreateUserDto = Omit<User, 'id'>;
type UpdateUserDto = Partial<Omit<User, 'id'>>;
type RoleCounts = Record<User['role'], number>;

async function load() { return { id: '1', items: [1, 2] }; }
type Loaded = Awaited<ReturnType<typeof load>>;   // { id: string; items: number[] }
```

{{diagram:derive}}

## Mapped types

```ts
type Nullable<T> = { [K in keyof T]: T[K] | null };
type Getters<T> = { [K in keyof T as `get_${string & K}`]: () => T[K] };  // key remapping
```

## Conditional types

```ts
type ElementOf<T> = T extends (infer U)[] ? U : never;
type A = ElementOf<string[]>;   // string
```

Conditional types **distribute** over unions when the checked type is a naked type parameter.

## Common mistakes

- Redefining DTO shapes by hand when they can be derived.
- Deep, clever conditional types that slow compilation and confuse readers.
- Using Omit on a union, which flattens it; use a distributive helper if needed.
- Assuming Partial is deep; it only affects the top level.
followUps: How would you write a DeepPartial type?
What is distribution in conditional types?
When is Record better than an index signature?

diagrams.title: Deriving types from one source
diagrams.alt: A base User interface is the single source; Omit, Partial and Pick derive the create DTO, update DTO and public profile types so changes propagate automatically.

questions.title: Interfaces vs type aliases: when do you use each?
questions.quick: For object shapes they are largely interchangeable. Interfaces support declaration merging and extend cleanly, and often give clearer error messages, so I use them for public object contracts and class shapes. Type aliases can name unions, intersections, tuples, primitives and mapped or conditional types, which interfaces cannot. I pick one convention per codebase, usually interface for object shapes and type for everything else, and enforce it with lint.
questions.revision: Interfaces merge and extend, suit object contracts; type aliases name unions, tuples and computed types; choose a team convention and lint it.
questions.detailed:
Both describe the shape of data. The differences are in **what each can express** and how they compose.

## Comparison

| Capability | interface | type alias |
|---|---|---|
| Object shape | Yes | Yes |
| Union, tuple, primitive alias | No | Yes |
| Mapped and conditional types | No | Yes |
| Declaration merging | Yes (same name merges) | No (duplicate error) |
| Extending | `extends` | Intersection `&` |
| Implemented by a class | Yes | Yes, for object types |
| Error messages | Often clearer named types | Can expand to long structural text |

```ts
interface Product { id: string; name: string }
interface DigitalProduct extends Product { downloadUrl: string }

type Id = string | number;
type Result<T> = { ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; error: Error };
type Pair = [string, number];
```

{{diagram:choose}}

## Declaration merging

```ts
interface Window { appVersion: string }   // augments the global type
```

This is how libraries are augmented. A type alias cannot do this.

## Practical rule

- Use **interface** for public object contracts, class shapes and anything consumers may augment.
- Use **type** for unions, tuples, function types, mapped and conditional types, and compositions.
- Be consistent. Mixed use is not a bug, but surprises readers.

## Common mistakes

- Believing one is faster or "more correct" universally; differences are minor and version-dependent.
- Using intersections of many large types where extends would give better errors.
- Accidentally merging two unrelated interfaces with the same name in global scope.
- Debating it in reviews rather than automating a convention.
followUps: How does declaration merging help library authors?
What happens when intersected types have conflicting properties?
How do you enforce a convention with lint rules?

diagrams.title: Interface or type alias
diagrams.alt: A decision flow: if the shape is a union, tuple or computed type use a type alias; if it is an object contract that may be extended or augmented use an interface.

questions.title: Which TypeScript strict mode flags matter most?
questions.quick: I enable strict, which switches on strictNullChecks, noImplicitAny, strictFunctionTypes, strictBindCallApply, strictPropertyInitialization, useUnknownInCatchVariables and alwaysStrict. The biggest wins are strictNullChecks and noImplicitAny. I add noUncheckedIndexedAccess for safer array and record access, exactOptionalPropertyTypes where the team can cope, and noImplicitOverride and noFallthroughCasesInSwitch. For legacy code I raise strictness gradually.
questions.revision: Enable strict, especially strictNullChecks and noImplicitAny; add noUncheckedIndexedAccess and noImplicitOverride; ratchet up gradually in legacy code.
questions.detailed:
The **strict** flag is a family; enabling it turns on a set of checks that remove whole classes of runtime errors.

## What strict includes (set may grow between versions)

| Flag | Protects against |
|---|---|
| strictNullChecks | Null and undefined slipping into values |
| noImplicitAny | Silent `any` from missing annotations |
| strictFunctionTypes | Unsound parameter variance in callbacks |
| strictBindCallApply | Wrong arguments to bind, call and apply |
| strictPropertyInitialization | Class fields never assigned |
| useUnknownInCatchVariables | Treating caught errors as safe |
| alwaysStrict | Emits "use strict" |

## Valuable extras (not part of strict)

| Flag | Effect |
|---|---|
| noUncheckedIndexedAccess | `arr[i]` and record lookups include undefined |
| exactOptionalPropertyTypes | Distinguishes missing from explicitly undefined |
| noImplicitOverride | Requires `override` keyword |
| noFallthroughCasesInSwitch | Flags accidental fall-through |
| noImplicitReturns | Every code path returns |
| forceConsistentCasingInFileNames | Cross-platform import safety |

```json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "strict": true,
    "noUncheckedIndexedAccess": true,
    "noImplicitOverride": true,
    "noFallthroughCasesInSwitch": true
  }
}
```

{{diagram:ratchet}}

## Adopting in a legacy codebase

Turn on one flag at a time, fix errors per module, and use a ratchet in CI so error counts never rise. Enabling strict globally in one pull request is rarely viable.

## Common mistakes

- Starting new projects without strict, then paying to migrate later.
- Silencing errors with `as any` or non-null assertions (`!`) rather than modelling absence.
- Assuming strict covers runtime data; external input still needs validation.
- Forgetting that `catch (e)` is `unknown` and must be narrowed.
followUps: What does noUncheckedIndexedAccess change in practice?
How would you ratchet strictness in CI?
Why is the non-null assertion operator risky?

diagrams.title: Ratcheting strictness
diagrams.alt: Enable one flag, fix errors module by module, record the error baseline in CI so it cannot rise, then move to the next flag until full strict mode is on.

questions.title: How do you avoid unsafe any using unknown, satisfies and type guards?
questions.quick: any switches off checking and spreads silently, so I avoid it. For values I cannot trust, such as parsed JSON or caught errors, I use unknown, which forces me to narrow before use. Type guards and assertion functions do that narrowing safely, ideally backed by a runtime validator. The satisfies operator checks an expression against a type without widening it, so I keep precise literal types while still catching mistakes. Lint rules such as no-explicit-any back this up.
questions.revision: Prefer unknown to any and narrow with guards or validators; satisfies checks shape while keeping precise inferred types; lint against explicit any.
followUps: What is the difference between a type guard and an assertion function?
When is as const useful?
How do you type untyped third-party modules?

diagrams.title: Untrusted data crossing into typed code
diagrams.alt: External data enters as unknown, passes through a guard or schema validator, and only then becomes a typed value used by the rest of the application.

questions.title: Why do you need runtime validation as well as TypeScript types (Zod, parse, don't validate)?
questions.quick: TypeScript types are erased at runtime, so they cannot protect against data from the network, storage, environment variables or users. I validate at every trust boundary with a schema library such as Zod, or class-validator in NestJS, and follow parse-don't-validate: the output of parsing is a new, precisely typed value, so downstream code never rechecks. I derive the static type from the schema with z.infer to keep one source of truth.
questions.revision: Types vanish at runtime; validate at trust boundaries with schemas, parse into trusted typed values, and infer static types from the schema.
questions.detailed:
The compiler checks your **code**, not the **data** that arrives while the program runs.

## The gap

```ts
const res = await fetch('/api/user');
const user = (await res.json()) as User;   // an assertion, not a check
```

If the server changes a field, the compiler is still satisfied; the failure appears later, far from the cause.

{{diagram:parse}}

## Parse, don't validate

Validation answers "is it okay?" and leaves you with the same loose value. **Parsing** returns a new value of a stricter type, so the type proves the check happened.

```ts
import { z } from 'zod';

const UserSchema = z.object({
  id: z.string().uuid(),
  email: z.string().email(),
  age: z.number().int().min(0).optional(),
});
type User = z.infer<typeof UserSchema>;

const result = UserSchema.safeParse(await res.json());
if (!result.success) throw new HttpError(502, 'Bad upstream response');
const user: User = result.data;
```

## Where to validate

| Boundary | Examples |
|---|---|
| Incoming HTTP | Body, query, params, headers |
| Outgoing responses from other services | Third-party APIs |
| Persistence | Documents read from MongoDB, caches |
| Environment | Configuration at start-up, failing fast |
| Browser | localStorage, URL params, postMessage |

## Choosing a library

| Library | Notes |
|---|---|
| Zod and similar schema libraries | Schema first, inferred types, works on both client and server |
| class-validator and class-transformer | Decorator based, natural in NestJS |
| JSON Schema or OpenAPI validators | Contract driven, language neutral |

APIs and defaults differ between versions; check the documentation of your chosen library.

## Common mistakes

- Using `as` on external data.
- Validating at the edge and then passing the unparsed original onwards.
- Maintaining a hand-written interface and a separate validator that drift apart.
- Returning raw validation errors with internal details to clients.
followUps: How do you validate environment variables at start-up?

How do you share one schema between client and server?

diagrams.title: Parsing at a trust boundary
diagrams.alt: Untrusted input is parsed by a schema at the boundary; failures are rejected with an error, and successes become a precisely typed value that the rest of the code trusts.

questions.title: How do you validate DTOs in NestJS with ValidationPipe and class-validator?
questions.quick: In NestJS I define DTO classes decorated with class-validator rules, and enable a global ValidationPipe with transform, whitelist and forbidNonWhitelisted. The pipe converts the plain body into a class instance, validates it and returns a structured 400 on failure, while whitelist strips unknown properties, which helps prevent mass assignment. Classes, not interfaces, are needed because decorators and metadata exist only at runtime. I derive update DTOs with PartialType and keep responses typed separately.
questions.revision: Use decorated DTO classes with a global ValidationPipe (transform, whitelist, forbidNonWhitelisted); classes carry runtime metadata, interfaces do not.
followUps: How do you validate nested arrays of objects?
How would you return a consistent error format?
Would you use Zod in NestJS instead, and how?

diagrams.title: Request validation in NestJS
diagrams.alt: An incoming request body passes through the global ValidationPipe which transforms it to a DTO class instance and validates it; failures return 400 and valid data reaches the controller.

questions.title: How do you share typed API contracts between frontend and backend?
questions.quick: I choose one source of truth for the contract and generate or import types from it. In a TypeScript monorepo that can be a shared package of schemas and inferred types. Across teams or languages I use an OpenAPI document or GraphQL schema with code generation for types and clients. Runtime validation still guards the boundary, and breaking-change checks run in CI. I avoid copying interfaces by hand, because they drift silently.
questions.revision: One contract source: shared monorepo package, OpenAPI or GraphQL schema with codegen; keep runtime validation and CI breaking-change checks.
questions.detailed:
A typed contract only helps if both sides **derive from the same definition**.

{{diagram:contract}}

## Options

| Approach | Strengths | Trade-offs |
|---|---|---|
| Shared package in a monorepo | Simple, one language, schemas plus inferred types | Couples release cycles, TypeScript only |
| OpenAPI spec with generators | Language neutral, docs, mocks, client SDKs | Spec must be kept truthful; code-first or spec-first discipline |
| GraphQL schema with codegen | Typed operations per query, fragments | Needs GraphQL stack; resolver types matter too |
| tRPC or similar end-to-end inference | No codegen, immediate feedback | Tight coupling, mostly TypeScript-to-TypeScript |

## Shared schema package

```ts
// packages/contracts/src/order.ts
export const OrderSchema = z.object({ id: z.string(), total: z.number(), status: z.enum(['pending', 'paid']) });
export type Order = z.infer<typeof OrderSchema>;

// server validates incoming bodies; client validates responses in a typed fetch helper
```

## OpenAPI flow

1. NestJS decorators or a hand-authored spec produce `openapi.json`.
2. A generator emits types and a client into a package.
3. CI diffs the spec against main and flags breaking changes.
4. Frontend upgrades the generated package deliberately.

## Governance

- Version contracts; deprecate before removing fields.
- Mark optional versus nullable explicitly.
- Do not generate types from live production responses.
- Keep generated code out of manual edits, and regenerate in CI.

## Common mistakes

- Hand-copying interfaces into the frontend.
- Trusting compile-time types without validating real responses.
- Sharing database entities as the API contract.
- Treating generated types as proof the server behaves as documented.

diagrams.title: Single source for the API contract
diagrams.alt: A contract source such as a schema or OpenAPI document generates types and clients for both the frontend and backend, with CI checking for breaking changes before release.

questions.title: How do you model errors in TypeScript: Result types vs exceptions and custom error classes?
questions.quick: Exceptions are untyped in TypeScript, since catch variables are unknown and function signatures do not list what they throw. I use exceptions for unexpected failures and programmer errors, handled centrally, and custom Error subclasses with a code and cause for classification. For expected, recoverable outcomes such as validation failures or not found, a Result discriminated union makes the failure visible in the type and forces callers to handle it. I pick one convention per layer.
questions.revision: Exceptions for unexpected failures with custom error classes; Result unions for expected, recoverable outcomes so callers must handle them.
followUps: How do you centralise error-to-HTTP mapping in NestJS?
How do you type errors across async boundaries?
When would you use a library for Result types?

diagrams.title: Choosing an error strategy
diagrams.alt: Expected outcomes such as validation failures return a Result value that callers must narrow, while unexpected failures throw custom errors handled by a central handler that maps them to responses.

questions.title: What are common async typing pitfalls in TypeScript?
questions.quick: The main pitfalls are floating promises that nobody awaits or catches, passing an async function where a void callback is expected, forgetting that async functions always return a Promise, using forEach with await, sequential awaits that should run in parallel, and asserting the result of response.json() without validation. I enable no-floating-promises and no-misused-promises lint rules, use Promise.all or allSettled deliberately, and type results with Awaited and unknown.
questions.revision: Avoid floating promises, async callbacks where void is expected, await in forEach and unvalidated json(); use Promise.all deliberately and lint the rest.
followUps: How do you limit concurrency across many promises?
What is the difference between Promise.all and allSettled?
How do you handle cancellation in typed async code?

diagrams.title: Sequential versus parallel awaits
diagrams.alt: Two independent calls awaited one after another take the sum of their latencies, while starting both and awaiting Promise.all takes roughly the longer of the two.

questions.title: What are branded or opaque types, and how do they protect IDs and money?
questions.quick: TypeScript is structural, so a UserId and an OrderId that are both strings are interchangeable and mistakes compile. A branded type intersects the base type with a phantom marker, such as string and a unique brand, making them incompatible. I create values only through a constructor or parser that validates, so a Cents or Email value is trustworthy by construction. For money I store integer minor units with a currency, not floating point numbers.
questions.revision: Brand primitives with a phantom marker so UserId and OrderId cannot be mixed; create via validating constructors; store money as integer minor units plus currency.
followUps: How would you integrate branded types with Zod parsing?
What are the trade-offs of branding every identifier?
How do you store and display money safely end to end?

diagrams.title: Branded types blocking mix-ups
diagrams.alt: A raw string passes through a validating constructor to become a UserId; a function expecting OrderId rejects the UserId at compile time, preventing swapped arguments.

questions.title: How do tsconfig and project references work in a TypeScript monorepo?
questions.quick: I keep a shared base tsconfig with strict options and extend it per package. With project references, each package sets composite true and declares its dependencies in references, so tsc --build compiles in dependency order, caches outputs through tsbuildinfo, and only rebuilds what changed. That also enforces boundaries, because a package can import only what it references. Workspaces link packages, and bundlers or test runners need matching path resolution.
questions.revision: Base tsconfig extended per package; composite plus references let tsc --build compile in order incrementally and enforce package boundaries.
questions.detailed:
In a monorepo, one giant tsconfig becomes slow and blurs boundaries. **Project references** split the program into independently built pieces.

## Layout

```text
tsconfig.base.json
packages/
  contracts/   tsconfig.json   (composite)
  ui/          tsconfig.json   references: contracts
apps/
  web/         tsconfig.json   references: ui, contracts
  api/         tsconfig.json   references: contracts
tsconfig.json  (solution file with references only)
```

{{diagram:refs}}

## Configuration

```json
// tsconfig.base.json
{ "compilerOptions": { "strict": true, "target": "ES2022", "module": "NodeNext", "declaration": true, "skipLibCheck": true } }

// packages/contracts/tsconfig.json
{ "extends": "../../tsconfig.base.json",
  "compilerOptions": { "composite": true, "outDir": "dist", "rootDir": "src" },
  "include": ["src"] }

// apps/api/tsconfig.json
{ "extends": "../../tsconfig.base.json",
  "references": [{ "path": "../../packages/contracts" }],
  "include": ["src"] }
```

Run `tsc --build` (or `tsc -b`) to build in dependency order with incremental output.

## Benefits and costs

| Benefit | Cost |
|---|---|
| Incremental builds and faster editor feedback | More config files |
| Enforced dependency boundaries | Must keep references in sync |
| Declaration output per package | Build step before consuming packages in dev, unless tooling maps sources |
| Parallelisable CI | Extra learning curve |

## Practical points

- Use package manager workspaces (npm, pnpm, yarn) to link packages by name.
- Align **module resolution** across tsc, bundler and test runner; mismatches are the usual source of "works in editor, fails at runtime".
- Avoid path aliases that only the compiler understands unless the bundler also resolves them.
- Task runners and build caches (such as Nx or Turborepo) layer on top.

## Common mistakes

- Forgetting `composite` or `declaration`, so references fail.
- Importing another package's `src` directly, bypassing the boundary.
- Committing build output or tsbuildinfo files.
- Using different strictness levels per package without a plan.
followUps: How do you make local development fast without rebuilding packages?
How do path aliases interact with bundlers and Jest?
When would you avoid project references?

diagrams.title: Project reference graph
diagrams.alt: The contracts package is built first, the ui package depends on contracts, and the web and api apps reference them; tsc build compiles in dependency order.

questions.title: How do you write type-safe React props and event handlers in TypeScript?
questions.quick: I type props with an interface or type for the component, reuse built-in types such as ComponentPropsWithoutRef for wrappers, and use discriminated unions for props that depend on each other. Event handlers use React's event types, like ChangeEvent of HTMLInputElement, or are inferred from inline handlers. Children are ReactNode. I avoid React.FC by default, avoid any for events, and use generics for reusable list or select components.
questions.revision: Type props with interfaces or unions, wrap native elements with ComponentPropsWithoutRef, use React event types, generics for reusable components.
followUps: How do you type a polymorphic "as" prop?
How do you type useReducer with discriminated actions?
How do you type context with a null default safely?

diagrams.title: Props as a discriminated union
diagrams.alt: A component receives props with a kind tag; the info kind needs only a message while the action kind requires an onConfirm callback, which the compiler enforces at the call site.

questions.title: What are declaration merging and module augmentation, and when do you use them?
questions.quick: Declaration merging means TypeScript combines multiple declarations with the same name, such as interfaces, or a namespace with a function. Module augmentation uses that to add properties to types from another module, for example adding a user field to Express's Request or extending a theme type in a UI library. It is useful for typing middleware-added data and global config, but it is global and invisible at the use site, so I keep it small, documented and in one place.
questions.revision: Same-name declarations merge; module augmentation adds members to third-party types, such as Request.user, but is global, so keep it minimal and centralised.
followUps: How would you type request-scoped context without augmentation?
Why must an augmentation file be a module?
How do you validate process.env at start-up?

diagrams.title: Augmenting a library type
diagrams.alt: A declaration file augments the Request interface of a web framework; the compiler merges the new user field into the library type so handlers can read request user without casts.

questions.title: How do you migrate a JavaScript codebase to TypeScript incrementally?
questions.quick: I migrate gradually while the app keeps shipping. Add TypeScript and a tsconfig with allowJs and checkJs where useful, get the build and tests running, then convert files in dependency order, leaves first, starting with shared utilities and API types. New code is written in TypeScript. Strictness is raised in steps, with a CI ratchet on error counts. I replace any with real types over time and add runtime validation at boundaries.
questions.revision: Add tsconfig with allowJs, convert leaf modules first, write new code in TypeScript, ratchet strictness in CI, and validate data at boundaries.
questions.detailed:
A big-bang rewrite stalls feature work. TypeScript supports **mixed JS and TS** projects so you can migrate file by file.

{{diagram:path}}

## Step plan

1. **Tooling**: install TypeScript and types for dependencies (`@types/*`), add a tsconfig with `allowJs: true`, and make the existing build and tests run unchanged.
2. **Soft checking**: enable `checkJs` selectively, or add `// @ts-check` and JSDoc types to important JS files to get value before renaming.
3. **Shared first**: convert utilities, constants and API types, since many files depend on them.
4. **Leaf-first conversion**: rename `.js` to `.ts` or `.tsx` for modules with few dependents, fix errors, then move up.
5. **New code in TypeScript** by policy, enforced in review.
6. **Strictness ratchet**: start lenient (`noImplicitAny: false`), then enable flags progressively, with CI failing if error counts or `any` count increase.
7. **Boundaries**: add schema validation for API responses and configuration, since types alone do not prove runtime data.

## tsconfig starter

```json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "allowJs": true,
    "checkJs": false,
    "noEmit": true,
    "strict": false,
    "esModuleInterop": true,
    "skipLibCheck": true
  },
  "include": ["src"]
}
```

## Handling pain points

| Problem | Approach |
|---|---|
| Untyped dependency | Install @types or write a small .d.ts |
| Dynamic objects | Record types, then proper interfaces |
| Large implicit-any areas | `unknown` plus narrowing, or temporary typed escapes with a TODO and tracking |
| Test files | Convert with the code they exercise |

Tools that auto-add types can speed up the first pass, but review their output; they often infer weak types.

## Common mistakes

- Converting everything with `any` and declaring victory.
- Mixing refactors and type conversion in the same pull request.
- Ignoring the build pipeline, so slow type checks block developers.
- No ownership or deadline, leaving the codebase half-migrated forever.
followUps: How do you track migration progress?
How would you handle an untyped internal library?
What do you do about build and test tooling changes?

diagrams.title: Incremental JS to TS migration
diagrams.alt: Tooling and allowJs come first, then shared utilities and types are converted, then leaf modules upwards, while new code is written in TypeScript and strictness is raised by a CI ratchet.

questions.title: What causes TypeScript performance and build-time problems, and how do you fix them?
questions.quick: Slow type checking usually comes from very large programs, overly complex conditional or recursive types, huge unions, heavy inferred types in public APIs, deep dependency type graphs, and checking declaration files in node_modules. I measure with tsc --extendedDiagnostics and --generateTrace, then apply fixes: skipLibCheck, incremental builds, project references, explicit return types on exported functions, simpler types, and separating type checking from transpilation using a fast transpiler plus tsc --noEmit in CI.
questions.revision: Measure with extendedDiagnostics and traces; fix with skipLibCheck, incremental and project references, explicit exported types, simpler types, and a separate typecheck step.
questions.detailed:
Compile time is affected by **program size** and **type complexity**. Measure before changing anything.

## Measure

```bash
tsc --noEmit --extendedDiagnostics     # files, types, instantiations, time
tsc --noEmit --generateTrace ./trace   # analyse in a trace viewer
tsc --listFiles | wc -l                # what is being included
```

{{diagram:tune}}

## Common causes and fixes

| Cause | Fix |
|---|---|
| Too many files included (tests, build output, node_modules sprawl) | Tight include and exclude; do not include dist |
| Checking all declaration files | skipLibCheck: true |
| Full rebuild every time | incremental plus tsbuildinfo, or tsc --build |
| One huge program in a monorepo | Project references, per-package builds |
| Heavy inferred types exported across modules | Explicit return types and named interfaces |
| Giant unions, deep recursive conditional types | Simplify, cap recursion, use interfaces |
| Large type-heavy libraries (query builders, schema libs) | Isolate usage behind typed wrappers |
| Duplicate dependency versions | Dedupe so types are not instantiated twice |

## Separate transpile from type check

Use a fast transpiler (for example SWC, esbuild or Babel) for bundling and dev servers, and run `tsc --noEmit` as a separate parallel step in CI and pre-commit. The bundler then does not wait on the type checker.

```ts
// public API: annotate, do not leave to inference
export function buildQuery(filters: Filters): QueryPlan { /* ... */ }
```

## Editor performance

- Open the workspace at the package level where possible.
- Limit auto-imports from huge barrel files; barrels also hurt bundling and tree shaking.
- Keep the editor's TypeScript version aligned with the workspace.

Available flags and tool speeds change across versions; benchmark on your own codebase.

## Common mistakes

- Guessing at causes instead of reading diagnostics.
- Disabling type checking altogether to "fix" build time.
- Adding clever type-level code for minor convenience.
- Relying on inferred return types across module boundaries.
